sermon:
There is a kind of letter you can only write about people you have watched. Paul has not seen the Thessalonians in months. He was driven out of their city under cover of night, dragged before officials, run out before the church was a season old. And yet when he opens this letter he does not begin with worry. He begins with thanks. He thanks God for a congregation he can read from the outside, the way you can read a tree by its fruit without ever digging up the roots.

**Faith that works, love that labors, hope that endures**

Paul names three things, and he names them by what they produce. "We give thanks to God always for you all, constantly mentioning you in our prayers, remembering before our God and Father your work of faith and labor of love and steadfastness of hope in our Lord Jesus Christ" (1 Thessalonians 1:2-3). Notice he does not praise their faith and their love and their hope as inner feelings. He praises the work, the labor, the steadfastness. Faith that does nothing is not the faith he is thanking God for. Love that costs nothing is not the love that proves a church. Hope that collapses under pressure is not the hope that anchors a soul. These three are inward, but they show. The town could see them.

And how did such a church come to be? Not by Paul's cleverness. "Our gospel came to you not only in word, but also in power and in the Holy Spirit and with full conviction" (1:5). The word came, but the Spirit came with it, and the people received it under affliction. That is the order Paul keeps returning to: God acted first. He chose them, the gospel came in power, and only then did the visible life follow. We get this backwards. We try to manufacture the fruit and skip the root. Paul will not let us. The labor and the steadfastness are real, but they grow from a soil God prepared.

**Waiting as the shape of their witness**

Then Paul tells us what the whole region was saying about them. They turned from idols "to serve the living and true God, and to wait for his Son from heaven, whom he raised from the dead, Jesus who delivers us from the wrath to come" (1:9-10). There it is, in the first chapter, the horizon the whole letter bends toward. These new believers were not waiting for a better economy or a quieter life. They were waiting for a Person to come back from heaven. Their hope had a name and a direction. And that waiting was not passive. It made them serve. It made them stand under suffering. The world watched them refuse despair and could not explain it.

I have to ask whether my own hope is visible like that, or whether I have quietly traded the return of Christ for a more comfortable now. It is easy to say I believe He is coming. It is harder to live so that someone watching me would conclude I am waiting for something. The Thessalonians did not argue people into the gospel. They lived as people expecting their Lord, and the report spread on its own.

**The Christ who delivers from the wrath to come**

Everything here rests on Christ. He is the Son God raised from the dead, which is why the waiting is not wishful. A buried hope cannot return. A risen Lord can. And He delivers us from the wrath to come, which means the church is not waiting in dread but in rescue. The day that terrifies the watching world is the day of our deliverance. That is why these believers could suffer and not break. Their future was secure in Someone who had already conquered the grave.

So the question this passage leaves on us is plain. Can the gospel be read in our lives without a sermon attached. Do we serve the living God and wait for His Son in a way the neighbors notice. The Thessalonians were a young church, persecuted and unsure, and still the whole region heard. Not because they explained their hope, but because they lived it.

Their waiting was their witness.

Every minister is eventually accused of something. Paul had barely left Thessalonica before the whispers started: he came for the money, he flattered the crowd, he was in it for himself, and now he has run off and abandoned them. So in this chapter Paul defends his ministry. But watch how he does it. He does not produce credentials. He does not list his training or his appointments. He simply reminds them how he came among them, because they were there, and they know.

**A ministry that hides nothing**

"Our appeal does not spring from error or impurity or any attempt to deceive, but just as we have been approved by God to be entrusted with the gospel, so we speak, not to please man, but to please God who tests our hearts" (1 Thessalonians 2:3-4). This is the hinge of the whole defense. Paul answers to God, not to the crowd. A man who lives for the crowd's approval will say whatever the crowd wants and shape his message to the applause. Paul says he was tested by the One who reads hearts, and that changes everything about how he spoke. He did not use flattery, he says, and God is his witness. He did not seek glory from people. He did not come grasping for what they had.

This is harder than it sounds, and I know it from the inside. The temptation in ministry is never to do something obviously wicked. It is to soften the edge of the truth so the room stays warm. It is to court the people whose approval feels like security. Paul names that temptation and says he refused it, not because he is impressive, but because he never forgot who was testing his heart. A minister who fears the congregation more than God will eventually betray both.

**Gentle as a mother, exhorting as a father**

Then Paul reaches for two pictures, and they are tender pictures. "We were gentle among you, like a nursing mother taking care of her own children" (2:7). And a few lines later, he was "like a father with his children" (2:11), exhorting and encouraging and charging them to walk worthy of God. A nursing mother holds nothing back. A father charges his children toward who they ought to be. Paul was both. He did not soften the truth, and he did not deliver it coldly. He gave the gospel with the warmth of a parent and the resolve of one who would not flatter them into ruin.

And to make sure they understood the cost, he reminds them: "We worked night and day, that we might not be a burden to any of you, while we proclaimed to you the gospel of God" (2:9). He made tents in the dark hours so that no one could say he preached for pay. He gave them the message and he gave them his labor, his exhaustion, his sleep. That is the line that exposes most of us. We will give people our words. We will give them our opinions and our advice. Giving them ourselves, our time when it costs us, our energy when we have none left, is the rarer thing.

**The minister who points past himself**

Why does any of this matter for a church learning to wait. Because the gospel Paul guarded is the gospel of the returning Christ, and a corrupted messenger corrupts the message. If Paul had preached for money or applause, the Thessalonians would have had every reason to doubt the hope he handed them. His integrity was not about Paul. It was about keeping the word about Christ clean enough to bear their weight when the Lord returns. He could call God to witness because he had nothing to hide, and a man with nothing to hide can point past himself to the One who is coming.

That is the call on every leader, and the indictment of every one of us who has ever shaded the truth to be liked. The question is not whether we are talented. It is whether we could let God test our hearts and let the people see how we came. Paul could. He gave them the gospel and himself.

He gave them the gospel and himself.

Paul is not embarrassed to tell us how much he hurt. He had been torn away from this church, he says, "for a short time, in person not in heart" (1 Thessalonians 2:17), and the separation was unbearable. He tried again and again to come back and could not. So picture the scene that drives this passage: an apostle, far from people he loves, who cannot get to them, who does not know if they have survived the storm of persecution, and who is slowly being eaten alive by not knowing.

**Love that cannot rest until it knows**

"When we could bear it no longer," Paul writes, "we were willing to be left behind at Athens alone, and we sent Timothy" (3:1-2). Read that slowly. To be left alone in a strange city is no small thing. Paul chose it. He gave up his only companion and stayed by himself in Athens so that Timothy could go and check on a church Paul could not stop thinking about. This is what real pastoral love looks like when it is not performing for anyone. It is the inability to rest while the people you love are in danger. Paul did not send Timothy to manage them or to collect a report for his records. He sent him because he could not breathe until he knew they were standing.

And his fear was specific. He was afraid "that the tempter had tempted you and our labor would be in vain" (3:5). Persecution does not only threaten the body. It pries at the soul. Paul knew that suffering can talk a young believer out of the faith, and he had no way to be there when the pressure came. So he sent the one person he could send and waited in dread.

**News that brings a man back to life**

Then the report comes back, and the chapter changes color. "Timothy has come to us from you, and has brought us the good news of your faith and love" (3:6). They are standing. They held. And Paul's response is almost extravagant: "For now we live, if you are standing fast in the Lord" (3:8). Now we live. Their faith was that much to him. His own well-being rose and fell on whether they stood. There is nothing professional or detached in this. A man's life is bound up with a congregation he cannot even reach.

I find that this exposes how thin much of my own caring can be. It is easy to care about people in a way that costs me nothing, to pray a quick prayer and move on, to be relieved at good news for an hour and forget by evening. Paul could not. He had tied his own joy to their endurance. He prayed "night and day" (3:10), not in a phrase but as a practice, asking to see them again and to supply what was lacking in their faith. That is love that does not let go.

**Standing firm until the Lord comes with all his saints**

And notice where Paul's prayer finally lands. He asks the Lord to make them increase in love and to "establish your hearts blameless in holiness before our God and Father, at the coming of our Lord Jesus with all his saints" (3:13). The horizon again. Paul does not want them merely to survive this round of persecution. He wants them established for the day Christ returns. Their standing now is rehearsal for their standing then. The whole reason their endurance means so much to him is that he is preparing a people to be found blameless when the Lord comes.

This is the love a church needs and the love most of us withhold. Not advice from a safe distance, but a shepherd whose own life is staked on whether the sheep stand, and who measures their standing against the return of Christ. Paul could not bear not knowing because he loved them toward that day. The question for me is whether anyone's standing in the faith is bound up with my own joy the way the Thessalonians were bound up with Paul's. It should be. Their standing was his life.

Their standing was his life.

At some point every honest believer asks what God actually wants. Not in general terms, but specifically, on a Tuesday, in the body and the bank account and the marriage. Paul does not leave the Thessalonians guessing. He tells them plainly, and the answer is not a feeling or an experience. "This is the will of God, your sanctification" (1 Thessalonians 4:3). God's will for this young church is that they be made holy, and Paul refuses to keep that word in the clouds. He brings it down to three concrete places where holiness is either real or it is nothing.

**Holiness in the body**

The first place is the body, and Paul is blunt. The will of God is "that you abstain from sexual immorality; that each one of you know how to control his own body in holiness and honor, not in the passion of lust like the Gentiles who do not know God" (4:3-5). Thessalonica was a port city, and sexual freedom was simply assumed, the water everyone swam in. Paul says the church is to be different at exactly this point, because the body is not neutral ground. To control the body in holiness and honor is part of what it means to belong to God. And he adds a sobering line: in this matter no one should wrong or take advantage of his brother, "because the Lord is an avenger in all these things" (4:6). What we do with our bodies is not private. It touches other people, and it answers to God.

I cannot preach this from a height. The culture Paul described is mild compared to ours, where the immorality he named is now a click away and treated as harmless. The church is no longer obviously different here, and that should grieve us. Holiness in the body is not a relic of an uptight age. It is still the will of God, and we have largely made our peace with ignoring it.

**Holiness in love and in labor**

The second place is brotherly love. Paul almost shrugs: "Now concerning brotherly love you have no need for anyone to write to you, for you yourselves have been taught by God to love one another" (4:9). They already love. His charge is simply to do it more and more. Holiness is not only restraint. It is increase. It is a love that keeps growing rather than settling at the level that feels comfortable.

The third place surprises people. Holiness shows up in how you work. "Aspire to live quietly, and to mind your own affairs, and to work with your hands, as we instructed you, so that you may walk properly before outsiders and be dependent on no one" (4:11-12). A quiet, diligent, self-supporting life is named here as part of God's will. Not flashy. Not impressive. A believer who works, pays his own way, and does not meddle commands the respect of the watching world and burdens no one. Holiness wears work clothes.

**Set apart for the Lord who is coming**

Why does sanctification matter so much in a letter about the return of Christ. Because the church that waits for the Lord is the church being made ready for Him. Holiness is not how we earn the day of His coming. It is how a people who belong to Him begin to look like Him before He arrives. The God who called them, Paul says, "gave you his Holy Spirit" (4:8), the very Spirit who makes the holiness possible. We do not manufacture this. We are being set apart by the One who indwells us, for the One who is returning.

So this passage refuses to let me hold faith as a private comfort while the body, the love, and the labor go untouched. God's will reaches the bedroom, the friendship, and the workbench. The church that waits for Christ is the church being made holy in exactly those places where the world expects no difference at all. We were not called to be impressive. God called you to be holy.

God called you to be holy.

Some questions you can only ask at a graveside. The Thessalonians had buried believers, and a terrible doubt had crept in. Christ was supposed to return. He had not yet. And now people they loved had died before He came. Were they lost. Had they missed it. Paul writes to crush that fear, and he does it with the most concrete hope in the New Testament. "We do not want you to be uninformed, brothers, about those who are asleep, that you may not grieve as others do who have no hope" (1 Thessalonians 4:13).

**Grief, but not without hope**

Notice what Paul does not say. He does not tell them to stop grieving. He tells them not to grieve as those who have no hope. There is a way for a Christian to weep that is different in kind from the world's despair, not because the loss is smaller but because the grave is not the end of the sentence. Paul grounds this in the resurrection: "since we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so, through Jesus, God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep" (4:14). The logic is simple and unbreakable. Christ rose. The dead in Christ are joined to Him. So they will rise too. Death has not stolen them. It has only laid them down to sleep until He comes.

Then Paul paints the day itself. "The Lord himself will descend from heaven with a cry of command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the sound of the trumpet of God. And the dead in Christ will rise first. Then we who are alive, who are left, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we will always be with the Lord" (4:16-17). The dead are not at a disadvantage. They rise first. And then the living are gathered to join them, and the whole company is with the Lord forever. "Therefore encourage one another with these words" (4:18). This is not speculation to argue over. It is comfort to hand to the grieving.

**Children of the day, awake and sober**

But if that day is certain, when is it. Paul refuses to set a date and instead changes the question. "The day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night" (5:2). For a sleeping world, it arrives as catastrophe, sudden destruction on people saying peace and safety. But not for the church. "You are not in darkness, brothers, for that day to surprise you like a thief. For you are all children of light, children of the day" (5:4-5). The point is not to calculate the hour. The point is to live as people who belong to the day even while it is still night.

So Paul calls them to stay awake and sober, and he arms them: "having put on the breastplate of faith and love, and for a helmet the hope of salvation" (5:8). Faith, love, and hope again, now as armor. The waiting church is not anxious and not asleep. It is alert, clear-headed, dressed for the day. And here is the foundation under all of it: God "has not destined us for wrath, but to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ" (5:9). The day that destroys the sleeping world is the day that saves us.

**The Lord who is the hope itself**

I feel the weight of this at every funeral I have ever stood beside. It is easy to recite resurrection in a sanctuary and harder to believe it with a casket in front of you. Paul does not offer a coping technique. He offers a returning Lord who descends, who raises the dead, who gathers His people, who will not be late by even one believer. The Christ who rose is the Christ who comes, and that coming is the answer to the grave. So we are permitted to weep. We are not permitted to weep as though the story ended in the ground. The thing the world cannot do, we are commanded to do: bury our dead and still hope.

Grieve, but not without hope.

Letters often slow down at the end, but this one speeds up. Paul has spent five chapters grounding a frightened church in what God has done and where history is going, and now he fires off a rapid round of commands, one after another, like a father at the door giving final instructions he cannot bear to leave unsaid. They come fast and short, and together they sketch the daily life of a people who are waiting for their Lord.

**The ordinary work of a waiting church**

First, how they treat one another. "We ask you, brothers, to respect those who labor among you and are over you in the Lord and admonish you, and to esteem them very highly in love because of their work" (1 Thessalonians 5:12-13). Honor your leaders, not for their titles but for their labor. Then he turns and aims at everyone: "admonish the idle, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, be patient with them all" (5:14). Notice he does not treat the church as a uniform mass. The idle need a warning. The fainthearted need encouragement. The weak need help. A waiting church learns to tell the difference and gives each person what that person actually needs, with patience underneath it all.

I find that line searching. It is easier to admonish the weak and coddle the idle, to get the prescriptions backwards because it suits my mood. Paul will not let the church be careless with souls. Different people, different medicine, and patience with every one of them.

**The constant posture of a waiting heart**

Then the famous triple command, three short sentences that have steadied believers for two thousand years: "Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you" (5:16-18). Always. Without ceasing. In all circumstances. Paul wrote this to people under persecution, who had buried their dead, who had every reason to despair. He does not tell them to rejoice when things improve. He tells them to rejoice always, because their hope does not rest on circumstances but on a returning Lord. This is not denial. It is the steadiness of people who know the end of the story.

And then a warning that matters: "Do not quench the Spirit. Do not despise prophecies, but test everything; hold fast what is good. Abstain from every form of evil" (5:19-22). A waiting church is neither gullible nor closed. It does not smother what the Spirit is doing, and it does not swallow everything uncritically. It tests, and it holds the good. That is a hard balance, and most of us tip to one side or the other, either suspicious of everything or undiscerning about anything.

**The faithful God who keeps us until He comes**

Here is the relief at the end of all these commands. If Paul stopped after the imperatives, this would be a crushing list, and we would fail it by Tuesday. But he does not stop there. "Now may the God of peace himself sanctify you completely, and may your whole spirit and soul and body be kept blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. He who calls you is faithful; he will surely do it" (5:23-24). Read that last line again. He will surely do it. The keeping is not finally up to us. The God who called this church is faithful, and He will keep them blameless until Christ comes. The commands are real, but they rest on a promise stronger than our performance.

That is the only ground I can stand on. I cannot read this list of commands and feel adequate to it. Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, hold fast the good, abstain from every evil. I fail these daily. But the chapter does not end on my failure. It ends on the faithfulness of the God who is bringing me, and bringing His whole church, to the day His Son returns. He started this. He will finish it. The church that waits does not finally keep itself.

The faithful God will keep you.
